sec.title: Background
sec.p: Behcet’s disease (BD) involves multiple immune cells, but the mechanism by which interferon α-2a (IFNα-2a) exerts therapeutic effects on BD through immune cell modulation remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the role of CD4 + IFN-I-related T cells in BD with active uveitis during IFNα-2a therapy.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: A single-cell atlas of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) was constructed from BD patients with active uveitis, post-4-month IFNα-2a therapy BD patients, active BD patients, and healthy controls (HCs) by integrating in-house and public scRNA-seq data. Bulk mRNA sequencing of CD4 + T cells from active BD patients and HCs was performed for validation. Cell-cell interaction, in vitro coculture, and inhibitor experiments were used to explore the underlying mechanisms.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: CD4 + IFN-I-related T cells (characterized by high interferon-related gene expression) were significantly decreased in active BD patients but restored after IFNα-2a therapy. The LLT1-CD161 interaction intensity between CD4 + IFN-I-related T cells and NK cells was reduced in active BD and recovered post-therapy. CD4 + IFN-I-related T cells inhibited NK cell activation and IFN-γ secretion via the CD161 receptor.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: IFNα-2a therapy reverses the decreased frequency of CD4 + IFN-I-related T cells in active BD, which in turn inhibits the inflammatory phenotype of NK cells through LLT1-CD161 interaction, providing new insights into the therapeutic mechanism of IFNα-2a in BD.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Behçet’s disease (BD) is a chronic recurrent multisystemic disease typically showing oral ulcers, genital ulcers, skin lesions and ocular lesions [1]. Uveitis is one of the most severe manifestations of BD, frequently leading to visual impairment and even blindness [2, 3]. Increasing numbers of studies have focused on the pathogenesis of this disease [4, 5]. The most widely accepted theories regarding BD etiology and pathogenesis are immunological abnormalities, genetic susceptibility, and environmental triggering factors [6–9]. Increasing evidence suggests that BD has dual features of autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases with abnormalities in both innate and adaptive immunity [10]. Dysfunction and imbalance of CD4+ T cells in BD have also been reported [11, 12]. However, a comprehensive elucidation of the multiple immune-mediated cell networks involved in BD has not been well addressed.

In clinical practice, systemic corticosteroids in combination with other immunosuppressive agents are used as routine clinical treatments for BD. However, corticosteroid resistance develops in some patients when this therapeutic strategy is implemented, and these patients may experience refractory uveitis as well as irreversible loss of visual acuity. In such cases, the combination of biologics therapy is alternatively used and may be associated with a beneficial result. Among all biologic therapeutic methods, recombinant interferon (IFN) α-2a has been identified as an effective and safe biological agent for treating refractory Behcet’s uveitis in some patients [13–15]. The therapeutic mechanisms of type I IFN in autoimmune diseases are multidimensional and include enhancing antiviral activity, inducing apoptosis, and regulating innate immune cell‒cell interactions [16, 17]. Specifically, some studies have reported that IFNα-2a treatment downregulates CD56+ CD16+ NK cells and γδ T cells in BD patients [18, 19]. The ratio of IL-10/IL-6 has been found to be increased after IFNα-2a treatment in BD patients [20]. However, there have been no studies concerning cell types and cell‒cell interactions in the immune system during IFNα-2a treatment.

In recent years, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has been developed and has radically changed the ability to synthesize gene expression patterns across a range of cell types in samples, improving the understanding of the heterogeneity of immune cells pathophysiologically [21, 22]. In this study, we performed scRNA-seq on PBMCs from 3 BD patients with active uveitis and PBMCs from these BD patients at 4 months after IFNα-2a therapy, and then integrated these datasets with multiple publicly available datasets to evaluate the abnormal immunophenotypes of BD and the cellular dynamics. We identified a decreased frequency of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells in active BD patients and recovery of this cell proportion after IFNα-2a therapy. Notably, we found an inhibitory effect of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells on NK cells possibly via Lectin-Like Transcript 1 (LLT1)-CD161 interaction in the BD patients during IFNα-2a therapy.

sec.title: Patients and sample collection
sec.p: Three patients who were diagnosed as BD with active uveitis at the First Affiliated Hospital of Chongqing Medical University were enrolled for scRNA-seq. As these three BD patients showed resistance to systemic corticosteroids and cyclosporine, treatment with subcutaneous IFNα-2a (3 million units per day for 4 months) was implemented. PBMCs were collected from three patients before and after 4-months IFNα-2a treatment. ScRNA-seq sequencing was conducted. Bulk RNA-seq was performed on sorted CD4+ T cells from other four BD patients with active uveitis and four HCs. For public data collection, scRNA-seq datasets of PBMC from 4 active BD patients and 4 HCs (GSE198616), bulk RNA-seq datasets of PBMC from 10 HCs and 9 active BD patients (GSE198533) and bulk RNA-seq datasets of skin tissue from 4 BD patients and 4 controls (PRJNA915044) were downloaded from Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database and Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database. To confirm the scRNA-seq results, we also performed flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and other cell biology experiments on samples from HCs, active BD patients with uveitis, and BD patients following IFNα-2a treatment.

BD diagnosis was made according to the BD diagnostic guidelines proposed by the International Study Group [23]. The enrolled patients with active uveitis were evaluated according to the Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) Working Group [24]. Patients with type Ⅰ or type Ⅱ diabetes, hypertension-related diseases, malignant tumors, viral infection diseases, other coexistent autoimmune or autoinflammatory diseases, or allergies were excluded from this study. Written informed consent was obtained from all enrolled patients. The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University Medical Ethics Committee (2021-KY-0585-002) and Chongqing Medical University Ethics Committee (No. 2018-048) approved this study. All of the procedures adhered to the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Single-cell preparation and RNA sequencing
sec.p: For scRNA-seq samples, 3 ml of venous blood from each enrolled patient was collected in an EDTA anticoagulant tube and processed within 4 h of collection. PBMCs were isolated from blood using Ficoll-Paque with cell viability exceeded 90%. The sorted PBMCs were washed and resuspended in PBS with 0.04% bovine serum albumin, loaded onto chromium microfluidic chips with 3’ chemistry, and barcoded with kit from 10X Genomics. RNA in the identified barcoded cells was reverse transcribed, and Chromium Single Cell 3’ v2 Reagent Kit reagent was used to construct sequencing libraries. Sequencing was manipulated on a sequencing machine (Illumina NovaSeq 6000, Illumina).

sec.title: scRNA-seq data processing
sec.p: Raw data originated from scRNA sequencing was performed using Cell Ranger software in linux system (version 6.0.1). The primary data were analysed using the CellRanger count commands. During cellranger procedure, qualification, screening, barcode enumerating and Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI) counting were used, and then quality control, clustering and statistical analysis were performed. Finally, genes were annotated using Ensembl build 93.

sec.title: Quality control of single-cell gene expression
sec.p: The raw gene expression matrixes generated from 6 samples of our local 3 BD patients before and after IFNα-2a treatment using CellRanger and the 8 samples from GEO datasets were imported into R software (version 4.0.2) and processed into Seurat object with the Seurat R package (version 4.1.0) [25]. First, the account of UMIs and the UMIs from the mitochondrial genome for each cell were counted. Next, the mean and standard deviation (SD) were calculated for UMIs and genes. Then, cells with total UMIs or genes outside the mean plus/minus two SD bounds were removed. Finally, cells with death and doublets in each sample were discarded using the “DoubletFinder” package in R software (https://github.com/chris-mcginnis-ucsf/DoubletFinder).

sec.title: Data integration, cell clustering, annotation, and proportion estimation
sec.p: The remaining 39,396 cells from the aforementioned 6 samples and 53,733 cells from the 8 samples in the GEO database were combined, and batch effects were removed using the Harmony package in R software. For each sample, gene expression matrix was combined and normalized to the read count, and cell cycle with calculated scores were identified using the “CellCycleScoring” function in Seurat package of R software. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed in 2,000 high-variable genes identified through “FindVariableGenes” in R software. Cell clustering was conducted based on the top 25 principal components using the graph-based clustering algorithm in the function “FindClusters”, with a resolution of 0.4. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) was applied to visualize the identified clusters. We then identified marker genes of each cluster to annotate the cell clusters. Specifically, highly differentially expressed genes in a certain cluster were identified by comparison with all other clusters using the Wilcoxon test in “FindAllMarkers” (min.pct = 0.25, only.pos = T, and logfc.threshold = 0.2). This procedure was used to identify the upregulated genes in each cluster. The parameter of this procedure is reported by Mayer-lab (https://rdrr.io/github/mayer-lab/SeuratForMayer2018/man/FindAllMarkers.html). Then some known marker genes of each cell subtype in these highly differentially expressed genes was chosen as cell markers, and the expression of marker genes in celltypes was visualized. The clusters of each cell were identified according to classical cellular markers. T-cell data were extracted and reclustered at a resolution of 0.1. The marker genes of T cell subtypes were used for identification. The proportion of each cell type was identified and visualized after annotation through the “ggplot2” package and R software. The marker genes in PBMCs and T subgroups were identified through the “scRNAtoolVis” in R software package (https://github.com/junjunlab/scRNAtoolVis).

sec.title: High dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA)
sec.p: To identify potential interferon-related genes module associated with the therapeutic efficacy of IFNα-2a in BD, we performed hdWGCNA by using the “hdWGCNA” package (version 0.1.1.9010) [26]. Briefly, for each cell population, we first subset the Seurat object for the cell population of interest and then performed the standard hdWGCNA pipeline by sequentially running the following functions with default parameters: TestSoftPowers, ConstructNetwork, ModuleEigengenes, ModuleConnectivity, and RunModuleUMAP. The correlation between the expression of specific gene models and disease status was calculated through Pearson analysis by “ModuleTraitCorrelation” method command.

sec.title: Pathway enrichment analysis
sec.p: In pathway enrichment analysis, Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analyses were performed to identify the involved functions and relevant signalling pathways in each cell type using “clusterProfiler” R package in R software [27]. Metascape online tools were also used to screen the pivotal changes in GO and KEGG terms [28]. Adjusted P values < 0.05 were used as the limitation of enriched pathways and biological functions. Hallmark pathway was used and calculated in GSVA.

sec.title: Trajectory analysis
sec.p: Pseudotime trajectory bioinformatical process was conducted with the Monocle 2 package in R software [29] to identify the differentiation of CD4+ T cell types. DDRTree algorithm was used in Dimension-reduction. Through this method, we identified two branches: one proinflammatory branch and one anti-inflammatory branch. The differentially expressed genes were then identified and analysed through GO and KEGG analyses as mentioned above. The result of trajectory analysis was verified through another R package “Slingshot” [30]. To manipulate Slingshot analysis, UMAP analysis of T cells was calculated, and naïve T cells were assigned as the beginning points in our current analysis. The spanning tree also supported the result as the existence of two branches, one proinflammatory branch and one anti-inflammatory branch.

sec.title: Cell isolation
sec.p: In this study, PBMCs were purified through Ficoll-Hypaque density gradient centrifugation from the peripheral blood from active BD patients and HCs. CD4+ T cells were isolated from PBMCs using the human CD4 microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany) and utilized for bulk RNA-seq, flow cytometry, immunofluorescence, and cell co-culture experiments. NK cells were isolated from PBMCs using human NK cell microbeads (Miltenyi Biotec, Bergisch Gladbach, Germany) following the manufacturer’s protocol and used for RT-qPCR, cell coculture experiments, flow cytometry, and cytokine detection.

sec.title: Bulk RNA library preparation and sequencing
sec.p: RNA purified from CD4+ T cells through TRIzol kit (Thermofisher, United States) was spliced into 250–300 bp short fragments using RNase R enzyme. These RNA fragments were manufactured as a template to synthesize following cDNA. The screened cDNA was processed into end-repaired alignment, a-tailed and ligated with sequencing junctions, and cDNAs of approximately 350–400 bp were screened with AMPure XP beads. cDNA strand with enrichment of uracil was degraded using USER enzymes. Then, cDNA libraries were constructed through PCR amplification. After the initial quantification by Qubit, the library was diluted to 1 ng/µl, and the insert size was detected by an Agilent 2100 bioanalyzer. The effective concentration of the library was > 2 nM, which ensured its quality. PE150 sequencing (Illumina, USA) was performed after the library was qualified.

sec.title: Bioinformatics analysis of the bulk sequencing data of peripheral CD4+ T cells
sec.p: For bulk RNA sequencing, raw data in FASTQ format were first processed through local Perl scripts. The Q20, Q30 and GC contents of the clean data were calculated. All downstream pipeline was calculated with clean and high-quality data. The reference genome database was constructed, and the reads acquired from last step were calculated through HISAT2 (v2.0.5). For downstream bioinformatics analysis, the count matrix was input into DESeq2 (v1.30.0) [31]. The standardized expression matrix was calculated with the variance stabilizing transformations (VST) function from Deseq2 R package. The expression of marker genes of IFN-I–related T cells, including IFI44L, MX2, IFI6, MX1, and ISG15, were used for clustering and visualization using the Pheatmap package in R software (v 4.0.2). For differential expression analysis, logFC > 1 and adjusted P value < 0.05 are set as the criteria of differential expressed genes.

sec.title: Bioinformatics analysis of the bulk sequencing data of skin samples
sec.p: The publicly available bulk RNA sequencing dataset of skin lesions from BD patients and skin samples from healthy control is downloaded from SRA database (PRJNA915044). Then, the following process was exerted as “Bioinformatics analysis of the bulk sequencing data of peripheral CD4+ T cells”. For differentially expressed genes analysis, |logFC|>1 and adjusted P value < 0.05 is set as the criteria of DEGs.

sec.title: Processing of PBMC bulk sequencing data from publicly available dataset
sec.p: Transcriptional profiling of PBMCs from 19 samples (9 aBD patients and 10 HCs) was downloaded from GEO database, GSE198533. The count matrix was calculated by DESeq2 package in R software [31]. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between the disease and control groups were identified with the criteria |log2 (fold change) |>2 (|logFC|>2) and adjusted p value < 0.05. Additionally, DEGs were visualized through the “ggplot2” R package in R software. Based on GO analysis of these DEGs, cell components, biological processes, and molecular functions were identified through the “clusterprofile” package in R software. Significantly enriched pathways of these DEGs were also screened through the “clusterprofile” package in R software [27, 32]. To evaluate the immune cell proportions in each sample, we converted the transcriptional profiles from count data to transcripts per million (TPM) values through the “countstotpm” function in the “IOBR” R package [33]. Then, we used 5 cell-type estimation algorithms through the “IOBR” package, including CIBERSORT-ABS [34], CIBERSORT [34], EPIC [35], TIMER [36], and ssGSEA [37], to infer the relative abundance of immune cells among PBMCs. For differentially expressed gene analysis, logFC > 2 and adjusted P value < 0.05 are set as the criteria of differential expressed genes.

sec.title: UCell, AUCell, ssGSEA and GSVA analysis
sec.p: For our current scRNA-seq data, UCell analysis was used to identify significant pathways in the T-cell subgroup, through “UCell” package in R software [38]. The “AUCell” R package was utilized to identify the activity scores of “responds to IFN-α pathway” in each cell subtype. By using the “ggplot2” package in software for visualization, the cells were divided into high-expression and low-expression AUC groups based on the median values of the AUC. Single-sample Gene set variation analysis (ssGSEA) or Gene set variation analysis (GSVA) was used to identify the biological pathways enriched in single-cell sequencing data of PBMC or CD4+ T cells [39]. All pathways involved in this study were screened in Gene Set Enrichment Analysis online database [40].

sec.title: SCENIC analysis
sec.p: PySCENIC (version 0.10.4) [41] was used in quantified and normalized expression gene matrix after being manipulated with Seurat pipeline, to predict regulatory factors of CD4 T cell subtypes using the default settings and the following cisTarget databases (https://resources.aertslab.org/cistarget/databases/homo_sapiens/hg19/refseq_r45/mc9nr/gene_based/) and cisTarget Human motif database v9 (https://resources.aertslab.org/cistarget/motif2tf/). Briefly, GRNBoost function was used to infer coexpression modules between transcription factors (TFs) and target genes, based on cellular gene expression correlations. RcisTarget was then used to refine the selected module by retaining direct target genes with the corresponding binding motifs of the TFs, and the results were visualized using “ggplot2” package in R software.

sec.title: Cell-cell communication analysis
sec.p: CellChat (v1.6.1) package in R software was adopted to analyse ligand-receptor interactions in multiple subsets of cells. The gene expression matrix of different cell subtypes generated by Seurat pipeline was used as the input file for CellChat [42].

sec.title: Establishment of the co-culture system
sec.p: CD4+ T cells from BD patients with active uveitis were isolated and treated with IFNα-2a (2000 U/ml; MedChem Express, United States) or PBS for 24 h. The CD4+ T cells were then collected and co-cultured with NK cells from BD patients with active uveitis as ratio of 1:3 for another 24 h. In receptor-blocking experiments, before co-culture with IFNα-treated CD4 T cells, NK cells were previously incubated for 30 min at 4 ˚C with 10 mg/ml neutralizing anti-CD161 monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) (clone DX12) or 10 mg/ml isotype IgG1 control antibodies (both from BD Biosciences, United States). Finally, cells and supernatant were collected and detected through flow cytometry and ELISA.

sec.title: PBMCs treatment and transfection
sec.p: The extracted PBMCs were cultured in Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI)-1640 complete medium, and treated with IFNα-2a (2000 U/ml; MedChem Express, United States) for 48 h. For STAT2 siRNA knockdown assays, PBMCs were transfected with RfectSP V2 siRNA Transfection Reagent (BioGenerator Biotechnology) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The primers of STAT2-human-2081, STAT2-human-239, STAT2-human-1225 are showed in Supplementary Table 4. To ensure the transfection efficiency, the mRNA expression of STAT2 in PBMCs were detected. PBMCs were then harvested 48 h after transfection for flow cytometry.

sec.title: Flow cytometry
sec.p: CD4+ T cells (1 × 105/500 µL) isolated from fresh samples and the transfected PBMCs treated with IFNα-2a were stained with surface antigen antibody CD4-APC (RPA-T4, 555349, BD Biosciences) in dark for 30 min at 4 °C. After washing with PBS, the cells were fixed and permeabilized according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Perm/Wash Buffer, BioLegend) and intracellularly stained with MX1-488 (EPR19967, Abcam) for 30 min. NK cells in the co-culture system were stimulated with Cell Activation Cocktail (with Brefeldin A, BioLegend) for 2 h, and stained for 30 min with the surface antibodies CD56-APC (B159, 555518, BD Biosciences), CD107-PE (H4A3, 555801, BD Biosciences), and T cell marker CD3-FITC (UCHT1, 555332, BD Biosciences). The stained cells were immediately detected through flow cytometry (Attune NxT, Thermo Fisher, USA), and analysed with FlowJo Software (version 10.8.1).

For fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), PBMCs isolated from 3 HCs were stained with antibody CD4-APC (RPA-T4, 555349, BioLegend) and MX1-488 (EPR19967, Abcam) as above methods. FACS was performed on BD FACSAria Ⅲ. CD4+MX1+ T cells were sorted as positive group, and CD4−MX1+, CD4+MX1−, CD4−MX1− cells were sorted as negative group for marker gene identification by qPCR.

sec.title: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
sec.p: IFN-γ secreted by NK cells was quantified using a sandwich ELISA Development Kit (R&D Systems, United States), following by the instructions of the manufacturer. The IFN-γ concentration of the supernatants was counted as the mean of five independent experiments replicates with standard deviation.

sec.title: Quantitative real-time PCR
sec.p: Total RNA of cells was extracted from 5 × 105 cells with TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, United States). The cDNA was generated using RT Master Mix (MedChem Express, United States) in PCR amplifier (LightCycler, Roche, Switzerland). The cDNA was amplified using SYBR Green qPCR Master Mix (MedChem Express, United States) following the protocol provided by the manufacturer. Quantitative Real-time-PCR amplifier (ABI Prism 7500 system, Applied Biosystems, United States) was used to obtain Ct values of each sample. The relative fold changes of indicated genes were determined utilizing 2-∆∆CT methods and normalized to β-actin.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence
sec.p: For immunohistochemical staining, CD4+ T cells from BD patients with active uveitis and HCs were prepared. CD4+ T cells extracted from PBMCs were spread over adhesion slides, and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde fixative for 10 min. The acquired CD4 T cells were rinsed with PBS three times, with interval of 5 min. They were then incubated in 0.1% Triton X-100 (Merck, Germany) in PBS for 5 min and blocked with 10% goat serum (ThermoFisher, United States) in PBS for 30 min. CD4+ T cells were immunostained overnight at 4◦C with primary antibodies anti-CD4 (1:100, PA5-87425, ThermoFisher, United States) and anti-IFI44L (1:100, PA5-65768 ThermoFisher, United States). The stained CD4 T cells were washed with PBS three times, and then incubated with secondary antibodies Cy3 anti-mouse (diluted in PBS, 1:100, P0193, Beyotime, China) and Alexa Fluor 488 anti-rabbit (diluted in PBS, 1:100, P0176, Beyotime, China) for one hour at room temperature, followed by another three times washing with PBS. Each slice was added dropwise to 50 µL DAPI solution (prepared with DAPI stock solution 1:500), protected from light nucleated for 5 min, and rinsed three times with TBST. Finally, the images were captured by a fluorescence microscope (DMi8, LEICA, Germany).

sec.title: Statistics
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed using R software 4.0.2 (The R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) and GraphPad Prism 9.00 software (GraphPad Company, San Diego, CA, USA). All statistical tests were two-sided according to data distribution. The groups being statistically compared showed homogeneity of variance. For two-group comparison in the study, two-tailed unpaired student’s t-test was performed. For pairwise comparisons among three groups, Bonferroni method was used for correction after multiple t test and the level of significance in double T test was indicated as P < 0.05/2. For multiple group comparison, ANOVA was also used and P values less than 0.05 were considered significant. Benjamini and Hochberg FDR was used in differential analysis of sequencing data (adjusted P value < 0.05). All results were averaged based on at least three independent experiments and were expressed as median and quartiles or mean ± SD.

sec.title: The landscape of PBMCs among active BD patients, BD patients after IFNα-2a therapy and HCs in single-cell solution
sec.p: The design of the study is shown in Fig. 1a. Specifically, we collected PBMCs from 3 active BD patients and obtained their PBMCs again 4 months after IFNα-2a therapy, and then performed single-cell RNA sequencing on the 10× Genomics platform (Supplementary Table 1). To improve power, we integrated these data with the publicly available scRNA-seq datasets (GSE198616) of PBMCs from active BD patients and HCs [43]. Taken together, our single-cell PBMC atlas totally contained 7 active BD patients, 3 BD patients after IFNα-2a treatment and 4 HCs. Another publicly available PBMC bulk sequencing dataset (GSE198533) from 9 aBD patients and 10 HCs was included analysis. The proportion and characteristics of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells were described through multifarious bioinformatical analysis. For validation, we performed bulk RNA-seq on CD4+ T cells sorted from 4 BD patients with active uveitis and 4 HCs (Supplementary Table 2). We also conduct differential gene expression analysis on public bulk RNA-seq dataset of skin samples from 4 BD patients and 4 control individuals. Additional samples from 31 HCs, 28 active BD patients, and 23 BD patients post IFNα-2a treatment were collected for flow cytometry and immunofluorescence (Supplementary Table 3). The inhibitory effect of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells on NK activity via CD161 was investigated through Cellchat analysis and in vitro inhibitor experiments.

sec.p: Single-cell data were acquired through 10× single-cell sequencing and integrated with the publicly available dataset. After quality screening, a total of 93,102 cells were retained for downstream analysis, with an average of 1,355 expressed genes per cell (Figure S1a). Thirty distinctive clusters were identified after the removal of the batch effect, dimension reduction, and clustering (Figure S1b). Sixteen cell types were manually identified by different marker genes (Fig. 1b), including CD3D and CD8A for CD4+ T cells and CD8+ T cells; CD14 and LYZ for CD14+ monocytes; KLRF1, GZMK and GZMB for NK cells; IL4R and CD79A for B cells, FCGR3A for CD16+ monocytes; PPBP for megakaryocytes; CD1C and CLEC10A for cDCs; CEACAM8 for immature neutrophils; LILRA4, CLEC4C and MZB1 for pDCs; HBA1 for erythrocytes; and SOX4 for HPSCs (Figure S1c). Figure S1d depicts the distribution of important markers. The dynamic variation in cell proportions among each individual from HCs, aBD, and postBD patients is shown in Fig. 1d, and that among each group is shown in Fig. 1e, with a predominance of lymphocytes. Additionally, we performed differential abundance testing on scRNA-seq datasets using miloR package to investigate the PBMC cell type composition between HC and aBD groups, aBD and postBD groups. The abundances of monocytes, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells and CD56dim NK cells were greater in PBMCs from active BD patients than in those from healthy donors (Fig. 1f, P < 0.05, log FC > 5). The abundances of cDC, CD16+ monocytes, plasma cell and CD56dim NK were decreased in BD patients after IFNα-2a therapy (Fig. 1g, P < 0.05, log FC > 5).

sec.title: Identification of the abnormalities in T cells in active BD pathogenesis
sec.p: To explore the important cell types involved in active BD, we first performed Weighted Gene Co-expression Network Analysis (WGCNA) on scRNA-seq data. The soft threshold power was selected as shown in Figure S2a. The cluster dendrograms were calculated and visualized (Fig. 2a). Specifically, seven modules were identified and the expression levels of Modules in PBMC celltypes were identified (Figure S2b & Figure S2d). Figure S2c shows the top 10 genes enriched in each module. The enrichment of interferon-stimulated genes, including IFI30, IFI44L, ISG15 and MX1, in Module 2 categorizes it as an interferon-related module (Fig. 2b). To investigate the relationship between the celltypes expressed interferon-related module and BD activity, the groups were ranked from 1 to 3 according to the activity of the disease, including 1: HC; 2: BD patients after IFNα-2a therapy; 3: active BD patients. We evaluated the relationship between the activity of the disease and each module in PBMC celltypes. As the heatmap shown in Fig. 2c, Module 2 exhibits a significantly negative correlation with the activity of the disease in CD4+T cells (R = 0.74, P = 0.01) and CD8+ T cells (R = 0.86, P = 0.05), and is positively correlated with the activity of the disease in CD16+ monocytes (R = 0.83, P = 0.03) and CD14+ monocytes (R = 0.68, P = 0.02), consistent with previous reports that IFN-related downstream signal transduction could induce the expansion of inflammatory monocytes [43]. This result suggested that the expression of interferon-related module in T cells is negative with the activity of BD, which might be a reason for the efficacy of therapeutic mechanism of IFNα-2a in BD.

sec.p: To further verify our current findings, we downloaded and analysed PBMC bulk RNA-seq datasets of active BD from GEO database [43]. A volcano plot for the differential analysis between PBMCs from active BD patients and HCs showed 284 significantly upregulated genes and 47 significantly downregulated genes (|logFC|>2, P.adj < 0.05, Fig. 2d, Supplementary Table 5). The DEGs were then explored through GO analyses. The results showed that DEGs were mainly enriched in “adaptive immune response” GO term (Fig. 2e). For the relationship and pivotal node of each term in GO analysis, “adaptive immune response” represented an independent factor and molecular biology direction in the pathology of active BD (Fig. 2f). These results suggested that abnormalities in T cells differentiation might be a pivotal factor in the development of active BD. Additionally, we aimed to identify cell types with significantly changed proportions in PBMCs between active BD patients and HCs using bulk RNA-seq data. Five algorithms for predicting cell types were used, and the most significant changes in the proportion of T subtypes among all PBMC subtypes in active BD are shown in Fig. 2g and Figure S2e-i.

sec.title: Dynamics of T cell subsets identified in scRNA-seq
sec.p: As described above, we discovered that the proportions of T cell subtypes were significantly changed in active BD patients. We further extracted T cell data from PBMC single-cell sequencing data and reclustered T cell subgroups. Nineteen clusters were regrouped, and each cell type was identified by using marker genes (Figure S3a & Fig. 3a), including CD3D and CD8A for distinguishing CD8+ T cells from CD4+ T cells, CCR7 for naïve T cells, GZMK and GZMB for CD8+ effector T cells, STAT5A for CD8+ STAT5A cells, NCR1 for NKT cells, MKI67 for proliferation T cell, GZMK for CD4 effector memory cells, IL17RA for CD4+ Th17 cells, GATA3 for CD4+ Th2 cells, TBX21 for CD4 Th1 cells and IFI6, ISG15, IFI44L and MX1 for CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells (Fig. 3b & Figure S3b). We also visualized the top 5 significantly upregulated genes in each T cell subtype (Figure S3c).

sec.p: The proportions of these T cell subtypes among the HCs, active BD and postBD patients were identified (Fig. 3c, Bonferroni-correction P < 0.025). Notably, among all T cell subtypes, CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells were the only one with a significant reduction in the active BD group (P = 0.0064) and were significantly upregulated after IFNα-2a therapy (P = 0.00026). To further investigate the differences in T cell subtype composition among the three groups, miloR package was used. The abundance of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells was significantly lower in active BD compared with HC (Fig. 3d, spatial FDR < 0.05), and their abundance increased in BD patients after IFNα-2a therapy (Fig. 3e, spatial FDR < 0.05). To support the result in the two scRNA-seq datasets, we analysis the proportion of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells in HC and active BD from GSE198616, and before and after IFNα-2a therapy Behcet uveitis (BU) from our single-cell sequencing data. The result showed a consistent tendency with the combined dataset in dependent datasets (Figure S3d, Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.025). The different expression patterns of upregulated genes in each cell type in the active BD patients were distinct from those in the HCs, and the expression patterns were reversed after IFNα-2a treatment (Figure S3e). Additionally, classical pathways related to T cell function were screened, and the scores of these pathways among T-cell subtypes was calculated (Fig. 3f), indicating that CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells exhibited a high response to IFNα in association with a decreased enrichment of inflammatory pathways.

To verify the downregulation of the markers identified CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells in active BD patients, CD4+ T cells from 4 active BD patients and 4 HCs were used for bulk RNA-seq. We performed a differential expression analysis between active BD patients and HCs (Fig. 3g, |logFC|>1, P.adj < 0.05), and four IFN-related genes, IFI6, IFI44L, ISG15 and IFI30, were shown significantly downregulated (IFI6: logFC= -1.10069, adj.P = 0.000533; IFI44L: logFC= -1.41431, adj.P = 0.000243; ISG15: logFC= -1.8959, adj.P = 0.007903; IFI30: logFC= -1.06162, adj.P = 0.048198; Supplementary Table 6). Besides, the standardized expression matrix was calculated, and the expression of marker genes by IFN-related T cells, including IFI44L, MX2, IFI6, MX1, and ISG15, was visualized and clustered through an unsupervised algorithm. The expressions of these marker genes in CD4+ T cells were significantly downregulated in active BD patients as compared to HCs (Fig. 3h).

To further investigate whether the downregulated markers of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells is a general event in other local tissue samples BD, we downloaded and analysed the DEGs of bulk sequencing data (PRJNA915044) based on skin samples obtained from skin lesion of BD patients and normal skin from healthy donors. The markers of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells, including IFI44, MX1, IFI44L, IFI6 was identified with significant downregulation (IFI44: logFC= -4.6818, adj.P = 1.9 × 10e-5; MX1: logFC: -4.29614, adj.P = 1.8 × 10e-5; IFI44L: logFC: -4.93715, adj.P = 0.000264; IFI6: logFC: -3.97337, adj.P = 0.012193 Figure S3f and Supplementary Table 7).

sec.title: The significantly reduced frequency of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells in active BD and recovery of these cells after IFNα-2a treatment
sec.p: The specific marker genes, IFI44L and MX1, were used to identify CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells for validation in extended sample. The purified CD4+ T cells were analysed by flow cytometry to detect CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells with the positive marker of MX1 (Fig. 4a). The results showed that the frequency of positive MX1 in CD4+ T cells significantly decreased in active BD patients as compared with the HCs (P = 0.0001), and significantly increased after IFNα-2a treatment (P < 0.0001, Fig. 4b). Flow cytometry and scRNA-seq showed similar proportions of these T cells. In addition, we sorted out CD4+MX1+ T cells by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) from PBMCs from 3 HCs. The relative expression of the hallmark genes IFI44L, MX2, IFI6, and ISG15 was detected by qPCR in CD4+MX1+ T cells compared to that in other cells in PBMCs (CD4−MX1−, CD4+MX1−, CD4−MX1+ cells). The relative expressions of IFI44L, MX2, IFI6, and ISG15 were significantly upregulated in CD4+MX1+ T cells than in other cells in PBMCs (IFI44L: P = 0.04; MX2: P = 0.01; IFI6: P = 0.02; and ISG15: P = 0.03, Fig. 4c). The results demonstrated that the hallmark genes of CD4+MX1+ T cells exhibited the same signature as identified by scRNA-seq.

sec.p: We also performed immunofluorescence on CD4+ T cells from HCs, BD patients with active uveitis and BD patients after IFNα-2a treatment. The specific marker antibody IFI44L was used, and its fluorescence was quantified. This result demonstrated a similar proportional trend in the proportion of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells, as revealed by scRNA-seq. (Figure 4d and e). The protein levels of the markers MX1 and IFI44L are consistent with the mRNA expression trend measured by scRNAseq.

sec.title: CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells are characterized by a partial anti-inflammatory activity and a strong response to type I IFN
sec.p: In further research, we focused on characterizing the identified CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells. UCell analysis was performed to estimate changes in hallmark gene sets in all T cell subgroups. We performed GSVA on CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells and visualized the pathways in hallmark gene sets. The results showed a downregulated expression of TNF-α/NKκB and PI3K/AKT/MTOR signalling pathways in this subtype (Fig. 5a). According to the quantification of the type I IFN enrichment scores, this subtype was identified as the most significantly increased subgroup among the CD4+ T cell subgroups (Fig. 5b and c, P < 2⋅10e-6). Additionally, the type I IFN enrichment score was significantly decreased in the aBD group but increased after IFNα-2a therapy (Fig. 5d, P = 8⋅10e-8). These results indicated that CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells exhibited partial anti-inflammatory effects and a strong response to interferon.

sec.p: To obtain a comprehensive understanding of the differentiation trajectories of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells among all CD4+ T cells, pseudotime analysis was performed using two algorithms, Monocle2 and slingshot. The pseudotime trajectory of CD4+ T cells showed two distinct routes in the Monocle2 analysis (Fig. 5e and f). Fate 1 mainly included CD4+ naïve T cells at the proximal branch, and Treg and CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells at the end branch. CD4+ naïve T cells and Tregs are two well-known types of CD4+ T cells with anti-inflammatory competence [44]. Based on these results, Fate 1 was identified as anti-inflammatory fate. Fate 2 including proinflammatory CD4+ T cells, such as CD4+ central memory T cells, CD4+ effector memory T cells, CD4+ Th1 T cells, and CD4+ Th17 cells was defined as a proinflammatory one. These definitions of Fate 1 and Fate 2 were further verified by slingshot analysis (Figure S4). We also identified differentially expressed genes and pathways between Fate 1 and Fate 2. The genes highly expressed in Fate1 exhibited naïve phenotype-related and anti-inflammatory characteristics, including CCR7 and LGALS2. The genes highly expressed in Fate 2 included numerous inflammatory genes, such as S100A8 and S100A9. After GO enrichment analysis of these DEGs, Fate 1 was characterized by increased expression of “negative regulation of leukocyte mediated cytotoxicity” and “negative regulation of leukocyte mediated immunity”, whereas Fate 2 was characterized as involving upregulation of “T-cell mediated cytotoxicity”, “positive regulation of leukocyte activation” and “I-kappaB kinase/NF-kappaB signalling” (Fig. 5g). These results from pseudotime analysis indicate that CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells have partial anti-inflammatory functions.

We further performed a transcription factor (TF) prediction analysis using the SCENIC package. The putative TFs of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells were ZNF557, ZBTB14 and STAT2, which were significantly different from those of other types of CD4+ T cells (Fig. 5h). To verify the effect of the transcription factor STAT2 on CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells, we stimulated PBMCs from BD patients with IFNα-2a in vitro. The expression of STAT2 is significantly upregulated with IFNα-2a stimulating (P < 0.0001) and significantly silenced by STAT2-siRNA-1 transfections (P < 0.0001, Fig. 5i). Flow cytometry was performed to detect the proportion of CD4+MX1+ T cells in lymphocytes. The results indicated that the proportion of CD4+MX1+ T cells significantly increased after IFNα-2a treatment in vitro (P < 0.0001, Fig. 5j), and silencing STAT2 significantly inhibits the proportion of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells (P = 0.005, Fig. 5k).

sec.title: The intensity of CLEC2D-CD161 interaction between CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells and NK cells is involved in BD pathogenesis and the therapeutic effect of IFNα-2a
sec.p: Dysfunction of cell-cell interactions is a pivotal pathogenic factor and is potentially used as a therapeutic target in multiple autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases. We further explored the potentially altered cell-cell interaction pairs between ligands and receptors in PBMCs. Cellchat analysis revealed the interaction intensity of different interacting pairs between CD4 subtypes and major cell types in PBMCs among HCs, active BD patients and BD patients after IFNα-2a therapy (Figure S5a). Notably, CLEC2D-CD161 pathway was found to be diminished in active BD patients and reversed in BD patients after IFNα-2a therapy (Fig. 6a). To identify the biological characteristics of NK cells in active BD patients, we performed GO analysis on the upregulated DEGs of NK cells in active BD patients compared with those in HCs in scRNA-seq data. The results showed that NK cells from active BD patients were significantly engaged in the “immune response-activating signalling pathway”, “activation of the immune response”, “regulation of tumour necrosis factor production”, and “tumour necrosis factor superfamily cytokine production” (adj.P < 0.05, Fig. 6b). We verified the expression level of IFN-γ and TNF-α in NK cells from 5 active BD patients with uveitis and 5 HCs. The result of rt-qPCR showed that the expression level of IFN-γ and TNF-α in NK cells from BD patients with active uveitis were significantly upregulated compared with those in NK cells from HCs (IFN-γ: P = 0.004 and TNF-α: P = 0.035, Fig. 6c), consistent with the result in scRNA-seq data (Figure S5b). Based on these findings, it is reasonable to presume that CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells could suppress the activity of NK cells through the CLEC2D-CD161 interaction.

sec.p: We further sorted CD4+ T cells and NK cells from active BD patients with uveitis and established a coculture system. The expression of various interferon-related genes, including ISG15, IFI6 and MX1, were upregulated in CD4+ T cells after stimulation with IFNα-2a (ISG15: P = 0.0023; IFI6: P = 0.0005, MX1: P = 0.0014, Fig. 6d). CD4+ T cells pre-stimulated with IFNα-2a could downregulate the frequency of CD107 positive NK cells (P = 0.0002, Fig. 6e and f), and could decrease the IFN-γ secretion of NK cells (P = 0.0006, Fig. 6g). To verify whether the deactivation of NK cells by CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells was mediated through CD161 receptor, a further experiment with a previously described coculture system was performed through blockage of CD161 receptor. Compared with that in the isotype control group, the activation of NK cells was significantly enhanced in the anti-CD161 group (P = 0.0077, Fig. 6h and i). The reduction of IFN-γ was found to be reversed in the anti-CD161 group (P = 0.0008, Fig. 6j). These results showed that the change in the CLEC2D-CD161 interaction pair between CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells and NK cells was involved in the therapeutic effects of IFNα-2a in active BD patients.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In the present study, we depicted single-cell atlas of PBMCs containing 7 active BD patients, 3 BD patients after IFNα-2a therapy and 4 HCs. Sixteen subsets were identified in PBMCs. A lineage of CD4+ T cells with high expression of ISGs, named as CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells, was identified with decreased proportion in peripheral blood of active BD patients and regained after IFNα-2a treatment. Using GSVA analysis, we found CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells with an inhibitory function on inflammation, and hyperresponsiveness to type I interferon. The LLT1/CD161 interaction pair between CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells and NK cells was declined in aBD patients and reverted after IFNα-2a therapy. Additionally, we verified that CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells could inhibit the activation of NK cells as well as the production of IFN-γ in active BD via the interaction with CD161 receptor in NK cells.

It is well known that T cells are involved in the pathogenesis of various autoimmune or autoinflammatory diseases [45]. A previous study using bulk RNA-seq on PBMCs from active BD patients showed that upregulated DEGs were relatively enriched in monocytes [43]. In the present study, we reperformed differential analysis on these datasets and expanded the inclusion of DEGs to identify the global biological process in active BD. GO enrichment analysis was performed and showed that T cell differentiation played a significant role in active BD. T cells are a heterogeneous population of cells with functional variations [46]. Previous study revealed abnormal differentiation of T cells into subsets such as Th1, Th2, Th17, and Treg cells occurs in BD [12]. Activated T cells are involved in the infiltration of the iris with Behcet’s uveitis [47]. All of these studies suggest that T-cell differentiation is involved in the pathogenesis of BD. Additionally, according to the result of ssGSEA and hdWGCNA, CD4+ T cells show a diminished response to interferons compared to monocytes in active BD. The reduced reactivity of interferon-related module in CD4+T cells connected with the activity of the disease, highlighting a specific immune dysfunction within this desease condition.

Single-cell sequencing has facilitated the resolution of the pathophysiologic mechanism of immune related diseases, including systemic lupus erythematosus [48], Sjögren’s syndrome [49] and rheumatoid arthritis [50]. Considering the pivotal role of T cells in active BD, we extracted and reclustered T cells from PBMC scRNA-seq dataset, providing insight into the heterogeneity of T cells and the pathogenic role of specific subtypes in active BD and IFNα-2a therapy. In the present study, T cells were redefined into 19 clusters. Among them, CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells with high expression of IFN related genes were identified with a significantly reduced proportion in aBD and reverted by IFNα-2a treatment. Our experiments verified the existence of this cluster and its proportion by examining expanded samples. Zheng et al. [43] also identified a cell type named “CD4+ T cells IFN related” in BD but without describing its proportion and function. In this study, pathway enrichment analysis showed CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells with downregulation of the inflammatory pathway and hyperresponsiveness to type I IFN. Trajectory analysis revealed CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells at the anti-inflammatory fate of T cell differentiation, with a similar differentiation pattern to Tregs, a well-known CD4+ T cell subtype with an anti-inflammatory phenotype. These results suggest that the dysregulation of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells may contribute to the pathogenesis of BD and serve as a therapeutic target in IFNα-2a complementary therapy.

In recent years, cell types expressing IFN associated genes have been increasingly reported, and high expression of type I IFN have been identified as a pathogenic factor for multiple autoimmune disease. Increased levels of type I IFN in cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE) and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) amplify photosensitivity of keratinocyte and aggravate skin inflammation [51]. Another study identified an interferon-related subtype, ISGhi T cells, enriched in SLE patients [52]. In dermatomyositis, Rice, et al. [53] found that a high frequency of ISG15+CD8+ T cells was associated with a poor survival. Interferon alpha contribute to the pathogenesis of Sjögren’s syndrome [54] and Systemic Sclerosis [55]. In this study, we showed a reduction of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells in active BD patients. Additionally, we revealed that type I IFN could inhibite BD activity in association with an increased frequency of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells. We have indicated that CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells could alleviate the production of IFN-γ and activation of NK cells. Consistent with other studies, a reduced expression of type I IFN cytokines in the blood of patients with active non-infectious uveitis [56] and a therapeutic effect through inhibition of IFN-γ expression have been reported [57]. These results collectively suggest that deficiency of type I IFN is involved in the pathogenesis in non-infectious uveitis. The reasons as to wether there is a paradoxical result concerning the role of IFNα in BD uveitis and other autoimmune disease is not clear. These results suggest that BD, which is often defined as an autoinflammatory disease [58], belongs to a distinct group of conditions. More studies are needed to clarify this issue.

While the aberrant differentiation of conventional pathogenic CD4 + T cell subsets, such as Th1 and Th17 cells, is an established pathogenic factor in Behçet’s disease, our study specifically validated the important pathogenic role of NK cells in Behçet’s disease. Previous studies have also highlighted the direct involvement of NK cells in the pathogenesis of uveitis [59–61]. Additionally, one study reported an increased number of IFN-γ-positive NK cells in the peripheral blood of patients with active Behçet’s disease [62]. In this study, through intercellular communication analysis and experiment validation, we revealed a significant alteration in the LLT1/CD161 interaction between CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells and NK cells during IFNα-2a treatment. NK cells are innate immune cells involved in early self-defense and cellular stress responses, participating in the inflammatory processes of the disease through their cytotoxic activity and IFN-γ secretion [63]. Therefore, demonstrating the modulatory role of this specific natural killer cell axis provides a unique and novel perspective on the therapeutic effects of IFNα-2a beyond the conventional Th1/Th17 paradigm. Consistent with these results, our analysis on scRNA-seq revealed that the expression of IFN-γ was significantly upregulated in all types of peripheral NK cells from BD patients, and downregulated after IFNα-2a treatment. These results indicated the expression of IFN-γ in NK cells from BD, and suggest that inhibition of IFN-γ production by NK cells might be one of the effects of IFNα-2a treatment.

Another intriguing result in our Cellchat analysis was that CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells could interact with NK cells via the LLT1/CD161 interaction, and the strength was decreased in aBD patients and reversed after IFNα-2a therapy. CD161, a newly identified inhibitory receptor on NK cells encoded by the KLRB1 gene, regulates immune homeostasis by inhibiting NK cell cytotoxicity and cytokine secretion [64]. LLT1, encoded by the CLEC2D gene, has been identified as the ligand of CD161 [65]. The LLT1/CD161 interaction has been demonstrated to regulate the function of NK cells pathophysiologically. Recently, an interesting study found that inhibition of CD161 could activate T cells and NK cells to produce proinflammatory cytokines and enhance the killing effect of these immune cells against tumors [66]. Białoszewska et al. [67] reported that the NKR-P1A(CD161)/LLT1 interaction could reduce lysis of normal articular chondrocytes by NK cells. In our study, co-cultured experiments verified that CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells could inhibit the activation of NK as well as the production of IFN-γ in aBD. Through blockage of CD161 receptor in vitro, we also verified that CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells could interact with NK cells via LLT1/CD161 interacting pair. In our study, we for the first time identified the decreased proportion of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells in aBD. The interaction between CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells and NK cells through CD161/LLT1 might be a potential therapeutic molecular mechanism underlying IFNα-2a therapy.

There are several limitations in this study. First, the characterization of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells identified in this study was mainly based on bioinformatics analysis and estimation of enriched pathways. Further in-vivo experiments on the characteristics and mechanism of anti-inflammatory effectors of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells are expected to be performed in future studies. Second, considering that CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells occupy a small proportion in the whole PBMCs and are difficult to be sorted from PBMCs, we sorted CD4+ T cells from PBMCs and stimulated them with IFNα-2a to mimic the phenotype of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells in vitro. This could lead to some compromise in the validation experiment. Third, we integrated the scRNA-seq data of PBMCs from BD with active uveitis and dataset of active BD patients to focus on the changes between BD patients after IFNα-2a treatment and active BD patients. The low amount of the samples, and the heterogeneity of the patients included in this study may yield a biased result. More studies are expected to clarify the changes in single-cell PBMCs atlas among BD patients with or without uveitis. Ocular tissue samples are also expected to identify the response found in Behcet uveitis. Furthermore, while our study elucidates the LLT1-CD161 interaction of CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells in peripheral blood, future investigations should explore whether a similar immunomodulatory axis exists locally within the aqueous or vitreous humor of patients with active uveitis. In addition, this study focused on the changes in PBMCs of BD patients before and after IFNα-2a supplementation therapy in addition to corticosteroid therapy. The effects of glucocorticoids on PBMCs during treatment deserve future exploration.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, the current study demonstrates the dynamic changes in BD patients during IFNα-2a therapy at single-cell resolution. The proportion of a subtype of CD4+ T cells, characterized by high IFN related expression, is significantly downregulated in active BD patients and reverted after IFNα-2a treatment. The LLT1/CD161 interaction between CD4+ IFN-I-related T cells and NK cells is a potential therapeutic mechanism for IFNα-2a therapy in BD.
